newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian forex rush points to naira devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian forex rush points to naira devaluation.

text.p: A surge in demand for hard currency by Nigerian banks points to a possible devaluation of the naira and a tremor for the military government's war on inflation, bankers said on Friday.
The central bank on Friday said demand at its weekly auction reached its highest level ever, touching $109.82 million from $62.49 million a week earlier at a rate of 85 naira to the dollar.

"The rumour in the market is that there will be a devaluation to 90 naira to the dollar when the central bank announces its rate for auction next week," said a forex dealer at one of Nigeria's biggest banks. Other dealers echoed the sentiment.
But the central bank quickly denied the rumours and talked up the naira's strength.
"There is no reason for devaluation and that is what the bankers have been told. There will be no devaluation," central bank spokesman Tony Ede told Reuters.

Bankers said reasons for a possible devaluation were more to do with speculation than any immediate increase in money supply -- particulary after the central bank increased sales of treasury bills to mop up liquidity.
"There is a feeling that the naira may not yet have found its level after the increase in money supply in March and April rather than in the last couple of weeks," said one banker.
"The possibility of the naira strengthening looks very unlikely and if there is a further devaluation we need to be cushioned, so we have to buy foreign exchange."
To prevent speculation banks have to prove that they have end users for the hard currency they are buying, but central bank officials privately admit it is difficult to control.
The military government has budgeted $2.77 billion for 1997 intervention on the autonomous foreign exchange market, giving a weekly average of around $53 million.
Heavily reliant on imports any loss in the value of the naira swiftly feeds through into an increase in consumer price inflation.
The cornerstone of General Sani Abacha's economic strategy has been the war on inflation and the weapons have been tight fiscal and monetary policies.
The 1997 inflation target is 15 percent from 28 percent last year.
But faced with a stagnant economy Abacha has also chosen to boost growth through reflationary spending and has targeted a rate of 5.5 percent against 3.25 percent last year.
"Clearly the government has been trying to target its spending sensibly and people are calling for growth but that may still mean losing out in controlling inflation," one banker said.
Nigeria relies on around two million barrels of crude oil per day for over 90 percent of export earnings.
